question: Control-wiring insulation resistance on a medium-voltage vacuum breaker shall not be less than:
choices: 2 MΩ
100 MΩ
500 MΩ
1 Ω
explanation: ATS 7.6.3.D.2 uses the same 2 MΩ control-wire floor as the low-voltage power breaker. The pole insulation is a different test and goes to Table 100.1 when the manufacturer is silent.

question: With no manufacturer contact-resistance band, a medium-voltage vacuum breaker pole is investigated when it deviates from adjacent poles by more than:
choices: 10% of nameplate
50% of the lowest value
explanation: 7.6.3.D.3 is the familiar 50-percent-of-the-lowest screen. The 10 percent figure is bushing power factor and capacitance. The pascal number is interrupter pressure, not microhms.

question: The magnetron atmospheric-condition test on each vacuum interrupter is:
choices: Required on every new bottle before any other test
Marked optional in ATS 7.6.3
A substitute for the contact-resistance test
The same test as a turns-ratio test
explanation: The MAC test carries the optional asterisk. The dielectric withstand across the open bottle is the integrity test that is written as a performed test. Do not skip the microhm check because a bottle “holds vacuum.”

question: Bushing power factor and capacitance on a medium-voltage vacuum breaker should stay within what percent of nameplate?
explanation: ATS 7.6.3.D.8 says within ten percent of the nameplate rating. Hot-collar results are compared with similar bushings on a milliampere or milliwatt basis, not forced into that same 10 percent sentence.

question: With no manufacturer vacuum number, interrupter pressure shall not exceed:
choices: 1×10⁻² Pa, and adjacent poles within two orders of magnitude
1 Pa, with poles matched within 1%
500 MΩ
explanation: 7.6.3.D.9 is 1×10⁻² Pa, and the poles shall not differ by more than two orders of magnitude. A bottle that is a hundred times softer than its neighbor is outside that screen even if you like the absolute number.

question: ATS 7.7 on a circuit switcher includes:
choices: Manufacturer SF6 pressure, electrical trip, and anti-pump
A network-protector phasing relay only
A battery specific-gravity test
A fiber OTDR
explanation: SF6 pressure and interrupter operation follow the manufacturer. Anti-pump, trip-free, and trip from each protective device are in the electrical tests. A circuit switcher is not a low-voltage molded-case breaker and it is not a network protector.

question: ATS 7.16.1.2 visual checks on a medium-voltage motor starter include:
choices: Dissolved-gas analysis of the contactor
Electrical and mechanical interlocks, plus barriers and shutters
A fiber OTDR
A network-protector phasing relay
explanation: The starter section tells you to prove the interlocks sequence correctly and that barriers and shutters are installed and working. Overload devices are set from the coordination study. Contactor insulation resistance, with no manufacturer voltage, uses Table 100.1.

question: The magnetron atmospheric-condition test on a medium-voltage starter’s vacuum interrupters is:
choices: The required pass/fail in place of contact resistance
Marked optional in ATS 7.16.1.2
A dissolved-gas test
Required before every across-the-line start
explanation: The MAC test carries the optional mark. Insulation resistance of the contactor is the test written without that mark. Do not skip the interlock and overload checks because a bottle is assumed to hold vacuum.

question: ATS 7.7 says circuit-switcher heaters and the electrical trip of the interrupters must:
choices: Be removed before the anti-pump test
Operate, and each protective device must be able to trip the switcher
Be tested as a flooded-cell battery
Follow the fiber bend-radius rule
explanation: Heaters are verified in operation. Each protective device is used to trip the switcher, and the electrical trip of the interrupters is checked. SF6 pressure remains the manufacturer’s number. Anti-pump is in the same electrical list.

question: Which item is NOT on the medium-voltage breaker electrical list in NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.4.5?
choices: Contact resistance and insulation resistance
Trip, close, and mechanism checks
Vacuum integrity and contact timing
Specific gravity of a flooded cell
explanation: Specific gravity belongs to stationary batteries, not to a breaker pole. The medium-voltage breaker list is contact resistance, insulation resistance, trip and close, the mechanism, vacuum integrity, contact timing, and enhanced overpotential, with control wiring that feeds solid-state parts left off the overpotential test.

question: Low-voltage and medium-voltage breakers in NFPA 70B-2026, when the manufacturer gives no interval, both fall on:
choices: 60, 36, and 12 months
12, 6, and 3 months
The vented-battery float row of 12, 12, and 1 month
Before each use
explanation: That is the ordinary standard row, and chapter 15 uses it for both voltage classes. The test lists are still different: low-voltage includes the 300 percent inverse-time test and three operations; medium-voltage includes vacuum integrity, contact timing, and enhanced overpotential. Sharing an interval does not mean sharing the test.

question: 15 kV-class metal-clad switchgear has a factory power-frequency withstand of 36 kV. The highest power-frequency withstand to apply in the field is:
choices: 36 kV
27 kV
18 kV
explanation: Field power-frequency withstand on metal-clad gear is limited to 75% of the factory value: 0.75 × 36 = 27 kV. 37.5 kV is the separate dc field value for this class. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.1.1.B.3 and Table 100.2 note 1; ref. IEEE C37.20.2-2025, 6.4 and Table 1.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.1.1.B.3 and Table 100.2 note 1; ref. IEEE C37.20.2-2025, 6.4 and Table 1

question: You want a dc field withstand on 27 kV-class metal-clad switchgear. What value applies?
choices: Use 37.5 kV, the same as the 15 kV class
No dc value is recommended for that class. Contact the manufacturer before applying dc
Use twice the rated voltage
Use 75% of BIL
explanation: The field dc table gives values only for the lower classes (20 kV for 4.76 kV gear, 37.5 kV for 8.25 kV and 15 kV gear). For 27 kV and above it gives no value, because dc voltage distributes unevenly. The manufacturer has to be asked.

question: Before a field dielectric withstand on a metal-clad lineup, which devices do you disconnect at their terminals?
choices: The main bus and the ground bus
The breaker secondary disconnects only
Nothing. Test the gear as assembled
Voltage transformers, control power transformers, and surge arresters mounted in the gear
explanation: VTs, CPTs, and arresters would either load the test set or be overstressed, so they come off at their terminals and are tested under their own standards. With dc, also short or disconnect wound-type CT primaries in the primary circuit. Source: IEEE C37.20.2-2025, 6.4.

question: A metal-clad breaker is racked partway, between test and connected. The interlocks should:
choices: Allow closing, since the shutters are open
Keep it from closing until it is fully connected or in the test position
Allow closing only by the manual push button
Trip the upstream main
explanation: One required interlock blocks closing unless the primary disconnects are fully engaged or a safe distance apart (the test position). Another keeps a closed breaker from being moved to or from the connected position. Check both before the gear is energized. Source: IEEE C37.20.2-2025, 7.10 items a) and b); 9.5.

question: Which feature makes switchgear metal-clad, and isn't required of all metal-enclosed gear?
choices: A fixed-mounted breaker bolted to the bus
Bare primary bus with no barriers between compartments
Fuses in place of a breaker
Primary bus and connections covered with insulating material throughout, plus automatic shutters over the primary disconnects
explanation: Metal-clad gear means a drawout interrupting device with self-aligning disconnects, grounded metal barriers around the major primary parts, automatic shutters, insulated primary bus, and mechanical interlocks. Fixed breakers or bare bus are not metal-clad. Source: IEEE C37.20.2-2025, 3.1 (metal-clad switchgear).

question: Acceptance testing a circuit switcher, the contact-resistance test is done on:
choices: The interrupters only
The isolating switch only
Both the interrupters and the isolating switch
Neither; only bolted joints are measured
explanation: ATS calls for a contact-resistance test of both the interrupters and the isolating switches, in addition to the low-resistance check through bolted connections. Without manufacturer data, investigate poles that differ by more than 50% of the lowest value. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.7.B.1, B.2 and D.2.

question: You read the circuit switcher operation counter at 1,204, run one close-open cycle, and read it again. A good counter now shows:
choices: Any value, as long as it moved
explanation: The counter must advance one count per close-open cycle. Record it as found and as left. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.7.A.12 and C.7.

question: On a circuit switcher, the optional insulation power-factor test is run:
choices: Only with the switcher closed
On each pole with the switcher open, and on each phase with it closed
Only on the isolating switch blades
On the control wiring
explanation: The ATS optional power-factor or dissipation-factor test covers each pole open and each phase closed. Results are compared with manufacturer data, or with similar units and test-equipment data. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.7.B.10 and D.10.

question: Metal-enclosed bus where all three phases share one enclosure but are separated by metal barriers is called:
choices: Nonsegregated-phase bus
Segregated-phase bus
Isolated-phase bus
Cable bus
explanation: Nonsegregated bus has no barriers between phases. Segregated bus adds metal barriers between phases in a common enclosure. Isolated-phase bus gives each phase its own housing with air space between. Cable bus uses insulated cables. ATS Table 100.17 lists different field withstand values by type. Source: IEEE C37.23-2015, definitions; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.17.
reference: IEEE C37.23-2015, 3 (types of metal-enclosed bus assemblies); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.17

question: The metal-enclosed bus withstand values in ATS Table 100.17 are lower than the factory values because:
choices: They are dc values
Field power-frequency tests on installed bus are limited to 75% of the factory test value
The bus is tested with the transformers connected
Field tests are 50% of BIL
explanation: Field power-frequency withstand tests on installed bus are limited to 75% of the factory value, and the ATS table applies that multiplier. The dc column is for reference only and does not mean a dc test is required. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.3 and Table 100.17 note 1; IEEE C37.23-2015, 6.4.3.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.4.B.3 and Table 100.17, note 1; ref. IEEE C37.23-2015, 6.4.3

question: An SF6 breaker has a gas sampling port. Under ATS 7.6.4 you sample the gas and judge it against Table 100.13. What do you not do?
choices: Test the sample against Table 100.13
Check alarm and pressure-limit switch settings
Break a sealed-for-life interrupter's seal
Leak-test the gas system using the manufacturer's method
explanation: Sampling is done only where a provision exists. ATS says not to break or distort sealed-for-life interrupters. Leak testing and alarm/pressure-switch checks are on the list. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.4.A.6, A.8, A.9.

question: After an SF6 leak test on a new breaker, ATS 7.6.4 accepts the result when:
choices: The leak rate is below 10% per year
Pressure loss is under 5 psig in a day
No SF6 leak is found
The density alarm hasn't operated yet
explanation: The acceptance criterion is simply no leak. Gas pressure and alarm settings follow the manufacturer's data. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.4.C.2.

question: SF6 purity is measured on a new breaker and again years later in service. Which pair of minimums applies under ATS and MTS Table 100.13?
choices: ATS above 98.5%; MTS at least 97.0%
Both at least 99.9%
ATS at least 97.0%; MTS above 98.5%
Both at least 95%
explanation: Acceptance gas has to be cleaner. ATS requires purity above 98.5%, and the MTS maintenance limit is 97.0% or more. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.13.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.13

question: A gas sample from a breaker in service shows 9 ppm SO2. How do ATS and MTS treat it?
choices: It fails both, since any SO2 is a failure
It passes both, since the limit is 50 ppm
It passes acceptance (under 10 ppmv) but fails maintenance (under 5 ppm)
Fails acceptance (under 5 ppmv) but meets MTS (12 ppm)
explanation: ATS Table 100.13 allows less than 5 ppmv SO2 in new gas, and MTS allows up to 12 ppm in service. Total decomposition products are similarly tighter at acceptance (7 ppmv) than in maintenance (50 ppm). Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.13.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.13

question: A GIS bus compartment with no switching operates below 30 psig. During maintenance, its SF6 moisture limit under MTS Table 100.13 is a dew point of:
choices: -36 °C (about 200 ppmv)
-23 °C (about 720 ppmv)
-10 °C (about 2500 ppmv)
-50 °C (about 40 ppmv)
explanation: MTS splits moisture by pressure. Below 30 psig (non-switching GIS) the limit is -23 °C (720 ppmv). At 30 psig and above it is -36 °C (200 ppmv), which also matches ATS. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.13.

question: A new SF6 breaker's gas measures a dew point of -30 °C. Against the ATS Table 100.13 limit of -36 °C, the gas is:
choices: Acceptable, because -30 is greater than -36
Too wet; a warmer dew point means more water
Acceptable, since dew point limits apply only in maintenance
Too dry, so it should be humidified
explanation: Dew point rises as moisture increases. -30 °C is warmer than the -36 °C limit, so the gas holds more water than allowed. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13; 7.6.4.C.1.

question: The gas handling cart used to fill a new breaker is oil-free. Under ATS Table 100.13, the oil-content test on the gas:
choices: Must be run at twice the normal limit
Replaces the moisture test
Is required only on breakers above 69 kV and on all GIS
Isn't required when handling gear is oil-free
explanation: Note 1 to Table 100.13 says oil content testing is not required when the gas handling equipment is oil-free. Mixed-gas breakers (note 3) go to the manufacturer's limits. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13 notes 1 and 3.

question: A new breaker uses an SF6/N2 gas mixture, and the purity reading is well below 98.5%. Under ATS, the right step is:
choices: Use the manufacturer's values for mixed gas
Reject it, because purity must exceed 98.5%
Accept it if the dew point passes
Top it up with pure SF6 until purity reads above 98.5%
explanation: Table 100.13 is written for SF6. Its note sends mixed gases to the manufacturer's data. Adding SF6 to a designed mixture would change its ratio. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.13 note 3.

question: IEEE C37.016 describes a circuit switcher with an integral isolating disconnect. In a coordinated disconnect operation:
choices: The disconnect and interrupter operate independently of each other
The disconnect interrupts the fault current first
The disconnect opens automatically after the interrupter opens
The interrupter can't open unless the disconnect is closed by hand
explanation: With coordinated operation, the disconnect follows the interrupter open to give a visible gap. With independent operation, disconnect position and interrupter position don't depend on each other. Source: IEEE C37.016-2018, clause 3.

question: A tech assumes the maintenance withstand for 15 kV metal-clad switchgear must be lower than the acceptance value. Comparing ATS and MTS Table 100.2:
choices: MTS lists 20 kV ac, three-quarters of the ATS value
ATS lists 36 kV ac, the factory value
MTS lists no ac value, only dc
Both list 27 kV ac; no further reduction
explanation: Both tables already include the 0.75 factor on the factory value and list the same 27 kV ac for 15 kV metal-clad gear. Unlike the recloser and sectionalizer tables, there is no second reduction. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.2; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.2.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.2; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.2

question: On a medium-voltage vacuum breaker, ATS 7.6.3 says critical distances such as contact gap are measured and judged against:
choices: Table 100.12
IEEE C37.04 default gaps
The manufacturer's published data
The adjacent breaker in the lineup
explanation: A.7 measures critical distances such as contact gap as the manufacturer recommends, and C.1 judges them against the manufacturer's data. ATS doesn't publish a generic gap. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.A.7 and C.1.

question: Which of these is a required (not optional) item on the ATS 7.6.3 vacuum breaker visual and mechanical list?
choices: Contact-timing test
Trip/close coil current signature analysis
Mechanism motion analysis
Thermographic survey
explanation: A.12, contact timing, carries no asterisk. Coil current signature (A.13), motion analysis (A.14), and the thermographic survey (A.16) are marked optional. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.A.12–A.16.

question: How does ATS 7.6.3 have you prove the vacuum interrupters themselves?
choices: Insulation resistance phase-to-ground with the breaker closed only
Contact resistance across each closed pole
A visual check for discoloration of the bottle
A dielectric withstand across each open bottle, done strictly per the manufacturer's published data
explanation: B.10 is the vacuum bottle integrity test: a withstand across each interrupter with the breaker open, in strict accordance with the manufacturer. The magnetron atmospheric-condition test (B.9) is an optional extra. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.B.9 and B.10.

question: A vacuum breaker with 125 V dc controls has no manufacturer coil data. Its trip coil operates reliably at 75 V. Using ATS Table 100.20, that is:
choices: A failure, since it must operate at 100 V or above
Acceptable, since the opening-function range for 125 V dc is 70–140 V
A failure, since trip coils must pick up at exactly 125 V
Acceptable only if the close coil also works at 75 V
explanation: B.4 tests minimum pickup on trip and close coils, using Table 100.20 when the manual is silent. For 125 V dc, the opening functions range is 70–140 V, while indoor closing and auxiliary functions run 100–140 V. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.B.4 and D.4; Table 100.20.1.

question: A 15 kV-class vacuum breaker has no manufacturer insulation-test values. Under ATS 7.6.3 and Table 100.1, the test is:
choices: 1000 V dc with 100 MΩ minimum
2500 V dc, with 5,000 MΩ as the recommended minimum at 20 °C
5000 V dc with 100,000 MΩ minimum
15,000 V dc with 1,000 MΩ minimum
explanation: B.1 tests each pole closed (phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground) and across each open pole for one minute. Table 100.1's 15,000 V row is 2,500 V dc and 5,000 MΩ. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.B.1; Table 100.1.

question: A 15 kV-class vacuum breaker's overall dielectric withstand has no manufacturer value. The maximum field-applied ac test from ATS Table 100.19 is:
choices: 34 kV
explanation: B.11 sends you to Table 100.19 when the manufacturer is silent. The 15 kV insulation-class row gives 34 kV factory, 20.4 kV maximum field ac, and 28.8 kV maximum field dc. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.B.11; Table 100.19.

question: Before a vacuum breaker goes back in service, ATS 7.6.3 has you trip it by operating each protective device. What does that prove?
choices: That the breaker's contact resistance is acceptable
That the vacuum bottles hold their withstand
That the coordination study is correct
That each relay or device actually trips this breaker through the real control wiring, per the system design
explanation: B.6 trips the breaker from each protective device and then resets logs and indicators. D.6 says protective devices shall operate the breaker per the system design. It's the end-to-end check that test-set injection alone can't give. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.B.6 and D.6.

question: The optional mechanism motion analysis on a vacuum breaker produces travel and velocity curves. ATS 7.6.3 judges them against:
choices: The manufacturer's published data
Table 100.20
The adjacent poles within 50%
IEEE C37.09 default velocities
explanation: C.6 holds travel and velocity to the manufacturer's data, and timing (C.4) and coil current (C.5) are judged the same way. Without that data the trace is a baseline for trending, not a pass/fail. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.3.A.14, C.4–C.6.

question: A medium-voltage air breaker is in the test position. Close and trip from the control switch both work. No one has tripped it from each protective relay, and the charge, trip-free, and antipump checks have not been done. What should you do?
choices: The control-switch trip is enough; relay trip paths can wait until first fault
Stay in the test position and complete a trip initiated from every protective relay assigned to the breaker, plus the charging, trip-free, and antipump checks, before you accept the breaker
Rack the breaker in and prove those functions live at full voltage
Skip trip-free and antipump checks on air breakers; they apply only to oil breakers
explanation: ATS requires, with the breaker in the test position, a close and trip from the control switch, a trip initiated from every protective relay assigned to the breaker, and checks that charging, trip-free, and antipump behavior all work. Those features must work as designed. Leaving them unproved is not an acceptable shortcut. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.6.1.3.B.4 and 7.6.1.3.D.4.

question: Contact-timing results on a medium-voltage air breaker do not match the manufacturer's published times, but the crew wants to accept the breaker because the open-close cycle felt normal. What is the right evaluation?
choices: Any timing within one second of the nameplate interrupting time is automatically acceptable
Timing tests are optional and may be omitted when the breaker opens by hand
Only close-coil current has to match the manufacturer; contact timing is informational
Do not accept the breaker on feel. Contact-timing values must agree with the times the manufacturer publishes
explanation: ATS includes a contact-timing test on medium-voltage air breakers and requires the timing values to agree with the times the manufacturer publishes. A subjective sense that the breaker opened is not a substitute for that comparison. Travel and velocity, when recorded, are judged the same way. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.6.1.3.A.15, 7.6.1.3.C.4, and 7.6.1.3.C.5.

question: Pole-resistance tests on a medium-voltage air breaker, with no manufacturer microhm limit in hand, read 28 microhms, 30 microhms, and 43 microhms on the three poles. What should you do?
choices: Investigate the 43 microhm pole. Without manufacturer data, ATS has you look into a pole that stands more than half again above the lowest of the adjacent or similar poles, and 43 is above that 42 microhm threshold
Accept all three; any reading under 50 microhms is automatically good
Reject the 30 microhm pole because it is not identical to 28
Average the three readings and compare only the average to 28 microhms
explanation: When the manufacturer does not publish a high-limit for contact resistance, ATS has you look into a reading that stands more than half again above the lowest of the adjacent or similar poles. Half of 28 microhms is 14, so 42 microhms is the investigate threshold. 43 exceeds that and needs investigation; 30 does not. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.6.1.3.D.2.

question: A field timing package is being run on a high-voltage circuit breaker after years in service. Which records does IEEE C37.09 call for, and what are they used for in this context?
choices: Travel-time curves are required on every breaker, including slow indoor units, and opening times are optional
These timing tests are only a factory development tool and have no after-service use

Record opening time on every circuit breaker, and record travel-versus-time traces on S2-class units whose interrupting time is three cycles or shorter. Once a breaker is already in service, those same records may be used to judge whether operation is still correct
Only a 60 Hz withstand test is used to judge whether an in-service breaker still operates correctly
explanation: IEEE C37.09 timing tests record the time to open, close, close-open, and reclose. Opening time is taken on every circuit breaker. Travel-versus-time traces are taken on S2-class units whose interrupting time is three cycles or shorter. The same clause notes that, once a breaker is already in service, those records may be used to judge whether operation is still correct. Source: IEEE C37.09-2018, 5.12.

question: You are measuring the closed-position primary-path resistance of a high-voltage breaker pole, terminal to terminal. What test current and what acceptance rule does IEEE C37.09 specify?
choices: Any convenient current below 10 A dc is specified, and a 50 percent pole-to-pole spread is the only limit
Use at least 1000 A ac, and accept any value under one ohm
Use 100 A dc or more and compare the result with the limit the manufacturer set for that rating; the measured resistance must stay within that limit
Path resistance is not a C37.09 test; only opening time is recorded
explanation: IEEE C37.09 requires the dc resistance of the primary circuit, terminal to terminal of each pole in the closed position, to be taken with a dc test current of 100 A or more, and the result must stay within the limit the manufacturer set for that rating. Source: IEEE C37.09-2018, 5.14.
